title: Miniature giants: investigating limb long bone structure in dwarf proboscideans
summary: Terrestrial vertebrates rely on their skeleton to provide structural support and allow the movement of the body. Heavy, graviportal taxa, such as extant elephants, exhibit numerous adaptive features in their bone anatomy enabling them to withstand their immense weight. Conversely, dwarfing events impose novel biomechanical constraints on the skeleton. The case of dwarf elephants raises the question of how graviportal animals adapt when undergoing drastic size reduction, and whether they retain graviportal features or exhibit paedomorphic traits. In this study, we examine the morphology and microanatomy of the six long bones in two fossil species of dwarf elephants, Palaeoloxodon tiliensis (adults) and P.___falconeri (juveniles), using both quantitative and qualitative approaches (3D geometric morphometrics, virtual slice comparisons, compact bone thickness cartographies). Our results show that in P.___tiliensis , the reduction in body mass is reflected in the morphology and microanatomy of the bones, suggesting a more flexed limb posture and a reduced parasagittal orientation compared to in fully graviportal proboscideans. Despite this shift, several key graviportal adaptations are retained in P.___tiliensis . Additionally, comparisons with early, non-graviportal proboscideans indicate that dwarf elephants exhibit a partial reversion to ancestral limb traits, while maintaining essential weight-bearing features. Finally, adult P.___tiliensis and juvenile P.___falconeri specimens exhibit a medullary area filled with trabecular bone, similar to that of extant elephants. Dwarf elephants are thus not scaled-down versions of their mainland ancestors, but instead display a combination of juvenile, graviportal and ancestral traits reflecting the impact of dwarfism on their evolutionary trajectory.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the morphology and microanatomy of long bones in two dwarf elephant species (Palaeoloxodon tiliensis and P. falconeri), finding that dwarf elephants are not scaled-down versions of their ancestors but exhibit a unique combination of juvenile, graviportal, and ancestral traits reflecting evolutionary adaptation to body size reduction.
AI.motivation: To understand how graviportal animals (like elephants) adapt their skeleton when undergoing drastic size reduction through dwarfism, and whether they retain graviportal features or exhibit paedomorphic traits.
AI.method: Examination of six long bones in two fossil dwarf elephant species using both quantitative and qualitative approaches, including 3D geometric morphometrics, virtual slice comparisons, and compact bone thickness cartographies.
AI.result: P. tiliensis shows reduced body mass reflected in bone morphology suggesting more flexed limb posture and reduced parasagittal orientation, yet retains key graviportal adaptations. Dwarf elephants show partial reversion to ancestral limb traits while maintaining essential weight-bearing features. Both species display medullary areas filled with trabecular bone similar to extant elephants.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf elephants are not simply scaled-down versions of mainland ancestors; they display a combination of juvenile, graviportal, and ancestral traits reflecting dwarfism's impact on their evolutionary trajectory.

title: The Connectome and the Quest for the Functional Logic of the Drosophila Early Olfactory System
summary: In recent decades, the early olfactory system (EOS) of the fruit fly has become a leading model for studying olfactory processing and associative memory, owing in part to a well-characterized feedforward pathway that feeds the processes underlying associative memory and by examining the role played by a handful of neurons and synapses. The recent completion of dense electron-microscopy connectomes provides high quality visualizations of every cell type, neuron, and synapse along the early olfactory pathway. Yet a wiring diagram, however complete, does not by itself reveal the functional logic of a neural circuit. Reviewing the EOS connectome and synaptome datasets of the past fifteen years, we note that the feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback circuits of large scale multi-input multi-output neurons. A systematic understanding of feedback loop abstractions, and their capacity to govern the input/output transformations at each neuropil stage, is the underlying foundation of the functional logic of the early olfactory circuits. In addition, we argue that a quantitative account of the functional logic requires an explicit model of the odorants present in the natural environment. Consisting of odorant objects, such a model defines the semantics and syntax of olfactory information processing, and calls for new distance measures for classifying the odorant semantics in support of associative memory operations. Furthermore, odor information processing must abide by causality, treating the circuit as a real-time, stage-by-stage cascade of giant local feedback loops.

AI.tldr: This review examines the fruit fly early olfactory system (EOS), arguing that despite complete connectome datasets, understanding its functional logic requires analyzing the dense local feedback circuits embedded within the feedforward pathway, modeling natural odorant environments explicitly, and treating the system as a real-time causal cascade of giant local feedback loops.
AI.motivation: While dense EM connectomes now provide complete wiring diagrams of the early olfactory pathway, a static connectome alone cannot reveal the functional logic of neural circuits. The authors aim to identify what additional frameworks and abstractions are needed to understand how the EOS processes olfactory information and supports associative memory.
AI.method: The paper reviews EOS connectome and synaptome datasets from the past fifteen years, highlighting that the feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback circuits of large-scale multi-input multi-output neurons. It proposes three pillars for understanding functional logic: (1) systematic abstractions of feedback loops governing input/output transformations at each neuropil stage, (2) an explicit model of natural odorant objects defining the semantics and syntax of olfactory processing with new distance measures, and (3) a causal, real-time stage-by-stage cascade treatment of the circuit.
AI.result: The review identifies that feedforward processing in the EOS is deeply entangled with dense local feedback circuits, and argues that functional understanding requires going beyond wiring diagrams to include quantitative models of natural odorant environments and causal temporal processing frameworks.
AI.conclusion: A complete functional account of the early olfactory circuit requires integrating connectome data with feedback-loop abstractions, natural odorant object models, and causality-aware temporal processing, forming a foundation for understanding associative memory operations.

title: Reducing Boolean Networks via Analysis of Dynamic Network Subgraph Behavior
comment: 33 pages, 6 figures, Check this Github repository for codes and more detials: https://github.com/jafarilab/BORNA
summary: Boolean networks provide a compact framework for modeling regulatory systems, yet their rapidly expanding state spaces make systematic dynamical analysis challenging. Here, we systematically enumerate all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory subgraphs with their admissible Boolean update rules and exhaustively characterize their state-transition graphs (STGs) under both synchronous and asynchronous updating. By extracting quantitative dynamical descriptors, we move beyond static wiring diagrams toward a behavior-based classification of network structures. The synchronous analysis identifies deterministic fixed-point and cyclic attractor regimes, while the asynchronous analysis captures one-node-at-a-time dynamics through terminal strongly connected components of the asynchronous STGs. Comparing the two update schemes distinguishes dynamical behaviors that are robust across update assumptions from those that depend on synchronous updating. Despite the diversity of graph-rule combinations, many realizations converge to a limited repertoire of dynamical classes, revealing substantial redundancy between structural and dynamical representations. We further propose a testable framework for investigating whether such local dynamical classes can be used to characterize selected subnetworks within larger Boolean models. To facilitate exploration and reproducibility, we developed BORNA, an interactive web application for exploring the complete network catalogue, STGs, and synchronous and asynchronous simulations, available at https://jafarilab.github.io/BORNA/. Together, these results provide a systematic reference for minimal Boolean network dynamics and a foundation for extending behavior-based analysis to larger regulatory systems.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically enumerates all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory Boolean networks with all admissible update rules and exhaustively characterizes their state-transition graphs under synchronous and asynchronous updating, revealing that diverse graph-rule combinations converge to a limited set of dynamical classes. The authors introduce BORNA, an interactive web application for exploring the complete catalogue of these minimal networks.
AI.motivation: Boolean networks model regulatory systems compactly, but their state spaces expand rapidly, making systematic dynamical analysis difficult. The authors aim to move beyond static wiring diagrams toward a behavior-based classification of network structures to understand how structure relates to dynamics in minimal regulatory subgraphs.
AI.method: The authors exhaustively enumerate all non-isomorphic two-node signed regulatory subgraphs with their admissible Boolean update rules, and characterize their state-transition graphs (STGs) under both synchronous and asynchronous updating. They extract quantitative dynamical descriptors including deterministic fixed-point and cyclic attractor regimes (synchronous) and terminal strongly connected components (asynchronous), and compare the two update schemes to identify update-dependent vs. robust behaviors.
AI.result: Despite the diversity of graph-rule combinations, many realizations converge to a limited repertoire of dynamical classes, revealing substantial redundancy between structural and dynamical representations. The analysis distinguishes dynamical behaviors robust across update assumptions from those dependent on synchronous updating. The authors also developed BORNA, an interactive web application for exploring the complete catalogue of networks, STGs, and simulations.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a systematic reference for minimal Boolean network dynamics and a foundation for extending behavior-based analysis to larger regulatory systems. The authors propose a testable framework for investigating whether local dynamical classes can characterize selected subnetworks within larger Boolean models.

authors: Isabel M. V. Guedes de Carvalho
title: Hepatitis C Virus Genotyping with a Transformer Neural Network
summary: This study aims to explore the applicability of Transformer-based models for genetic sequence classification by evaluating their performance in predicting hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotypes and subtypes after fine-tuning. A total of 2,881 HCV whole-genome sequences obtained from the Los Alamos HCV Sequence Database were used, including genotypes 1 to 6 and all confirmed subtypes. Genotypes 7 and 8 were excluded due to an insufficient number of samples. The fine-tuning process was based on several datasets that differed in fragmentation method, data volume per file, and labeling. In genotype classification, fine-tuning strategies employing homogeneous fragmentation and balanced sample distribution resulted in higher performance, with precision ranging from 98.48% to 100%. In contrast, fine-tuning conducted using a fragmentation strategy that caused data imbalance, along with an arbitrary distribution of samples across training files, achieved a precision of 48.12%, which is considered low compared with other models. This configuration, which was also manually evaluated, resulted in a high error rate in genotype 5 prediction due to its low frequency in the datasets used. In subtype classification, the best-performing fine-tuning approach achieved 99.89% accuracy and 99.87% precision. Models that included additional genotypes showed a slight decrease in performance due to the increased complexity of the task. This study demonstrates that, when fine-tuning datasets contain properly fragmented, distributed, and labeled genetic sequences, Transformer-based neural networks can achieve high performance and are a promising approach for HCV genotype and subtype classification.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates fine-tuned Transformer-based models for classifying HCV genotypes and subtypes using 2,881 whole-genome sequences. Proper dataset fragmentation, balanced distribution, and labeling during fine-tuning yield high performance (98.48%-100% precision for genotypes, 99.89% accuracy for subtypes), while poor fragmentation causing data imbalance drastically reduces precision to 48.12%.
AI.motivation: To explore whether Transformer-based neural networks can be effectively applied to genetic sequence classification, specifically for HCV genotype and subtype prediction, and to assess how fine-tuning data preparation strategies impact model performance.
AI.method: Transformer-based models were fine-tuned on 2,881 HCV whole-genome sequences (genotypes 1-6, all confirmed subtypes) from the Los Alamos HCV Sequence Database. Multiple fine-tuning datasets were created varying in fragmentation method, data volume per file, and labeling strategy. Performance was compared across genotype and subtype classification tasks.
AI.result: Genotype classification achieved 98.48%-100% precision with homogeneous fragmentation and balanced sample distribution, but only 48.12% precision with imbalanced fragmentation. Subtype classification achieved 99.89% accuracy and 99.87% precision with the best configuration. Models including additional genotypes showed slightly reduced performance due to increased complexity.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based models are a promising approach for HCV genotype and subtype classification, provided that fine-tuning datasets are properly fragmented, distributed, and labeled. Data preparation quality, especially sample balance, is critical to achieving high classification accuracy.

title: A stochastic dose-response framework for environmentally persistent pathogens
summary: Infectious diseases caused by environmentally persistent pathogens can strongly affect host populations as transmission occurs not only through direct host-host contact but also via indirect exposure to contaminated environments. While in some systems environmental reservoirs help sustain exposure even when infected host numbers are low, reliance on environmental transmission pathway may also increase pathogen extinction risk. Infection risk may depend on both pathogen dose and timing of exposure. Thus, understanding how dose-response, stochasticity, and seasonal changes in host susceptibility or contact rates shape pathogen invasion and persistence remains an important challenge for environmentally transmitted disease systems. To address this, we develop a stochastic dose-response framework that integrates host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir. Transmission occurs through both direct contact with infectious hosts and indirect environmental exposure, with infection probability governed by dose-response functions. We focus on stochastic continuous-time Markov chain formulation and use branching process approximation to estimate disease extinction probabilities when infected hosts or environmental pathogen loads are low. We extend the framework to include seasonality in host susceptibility, environmental contact, and host-host contact. As a case study, we apply the model to snake fungal disease. Numerical simulations show that dose-response influences epidemic takeoff and infection levels, while seasonality creates windows of high and low extinction risk. These extinction risks depend strongly on the route and timing of introduction within the seasonal cycle. These results, coupled with global sensitivity analysis, illustrate how stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing shape outbreak dynamics for environmentally persistent pathogens.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a stochastic dose-response framework for environmentally transmitted infectious diseases, integrating host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir. Using continuous-time Markov chain formulations and branching process approximations, the authors estimate extinction probabilities and incorporate seasonality in host susceptibility and contact rates. The framework is applied to snake fungal disease, showing that dose-response, stochasticity, and seasonal timing critically shape outbreak dynamics and extinction risk.
AI.motivation: Environmentally persistent pathogens pose unique challenges because transmission occurs through both direct contact and indirect environmental exposure. Understanding how dose-response relationships, stochasticity, and seasonal variation affect pathogen invasion and persistence is critical but remains poorly understood, particularly for systems where environmental reservoirs are central to transmission dynamics.
AI.method: The authors develop a stochastic framework based on continuous-time Markov chains that integrates host infection dynamics with an explicit environmental pathogen reservoir. Transmission includes both direct host-host contact and indirect environmental exposure, with infection probability governed by dose-response functions. Branching process approximations are used to estimate extinction probabilities when host numbers or environmental pathogen loads are low, and the framework is extended to incorporate seasonality in host susceptibility, environmental contact, and host-host contact rates. The model is applied to snake fungal disease as a case study, with global sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate that dose-response relationships influence epidemic takeoff and infection levels, while seasonality creates time-dependent windows of high and low extinction risk. Extinction risks depend strongly on the route and timing of pathogen introduction within the seasonal cycle. Global sensitivity analysis further reveals how stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response, and seasonal timing jointly shape outbreak dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The study illustrates that for environmentally transmitted pathogens, outbreak dynamics and extinction risk are governed by the interplay of stochasticity, nonlinear dose-response relationships, and seasonal timing. This framework provides a systematic approach for assessing invasion and persistence risks in environmentally persistent pathogen systems.

title: Correlations at criticality in ecological communities
summary: Ecological communities are continually reshaped by invasion, exclusion, and diversification, processes that naturally drive them toward the boundary of dynamical stability. Near such a boundary, a soft mode relaxes increasingly slowly and, under stochastic forcing, is expected to dominate the fluctuations, effectively reducing the dynamics to one dimension and generating strong positive and negative abundance correlations. Such correlations have therefore been proposed as signatures of an imminent transition. Here we show that this expectation can fail even arbitrarily close to criticality. The reason is that spectral softness does not guarantee stochastic visibility: the soft mode must receive enough environmental forcing to dominate the fluctuation background generated by the remaining modes. We demonstrate this mechanism in three ecological scenarios: a synthetic feasible community, a local community assembled by immigration from a regional pool, and a community generated by repeated diversification. In all three, communities approach marginal stability without developing the near-perfect pairwise correlations predicted by the single-mode picture. Thus, proximity to ecological criticality need not be visible in equal-time pairwise correlations.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that ecological communities approaching critical stability may not exhibit the predicted strong pairwise abundance correlations, because spectral softness does not guarantee that the soft mode dominates observable fluctuations under stochastic forcing.
AI.motivation: Ecological communities naturally evolve toward dynamical stability boundaries, where conventional theory predicts a soft mode should dominate fluctuations and generate strong positive/negative correlations. These correlations have been proposed as early-warning signatures of imminent transitions, but this expectation may be flawed.
AI.method: The authors analyze the mismatch between spectral softness and stochastic visibility of the soft mode, demonstrating this mechanism in three ecological scenarios: a synthetic feasible community, a local community assembled by immigration from a regional pool, and a community generated by repeated diversification.
AI.result: In all three scenarios, communities approach marginal stability without developing the near-perfect pairwise correlations predicted by the single-mode picture, showing that spectral softness does not guarantee stochastic visibility.
AI.conclusion: Proximity to ecological criticality need not be visible in equal-time pairwise correlations, challenging the use of such correlations as reliable signatures of imminent ecological transitions.

title: PEtab SciML: an exchange format for specifying and training dynamic scientific machine learning models
summary: Summary: Dynamic scientific machine learning (SciML) models that combine mechanistic ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with machine learning (ML) components have applications ranging from learning unknown biological processes to integrating auxiliary data modalities into dynamic modelling. To enable reproducible and efficient SciML training, we introduce PEtab SciML, an interoperable data format for specifying parameter estimation problems in which mechanistic and ML model parameters are jointly estimated from time series data. PEtab SciML supports several ML ODE hybridization patterns in realistic problem setups. It is accompanied by a reference Python library and downstream modelling support in Python/JAX and Julia, provided by AMICI and PEtab.jl, respectively, and a collection of real data benchmarks. Availability and implementation: PEtab SciML is available on GitHub (https://github.com/PEtab-dev/petab_sciml). The reference Python package is installable from PyPI and is continuously tested and supported on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

AI.tldr: PEtab SciML is an interoperable data format for specifying parameter estimation problems in dynamic scientific machine learning, where mechanistic ODE models and machine learning components are jointly estimated from time series data. It includes a reference Python library, support in Python/JAX and Julia (via AMICI and PEtab.jl), and real data benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To enable reproducible and efficient training of dynamic SciML models that combine mechanistic ODEs with ML components (e.g., learning unknown biological processes or integrating auxiliary data modalities).
AI.method: Introduces PEtab SciML, an interoperable data format for specifying parameter estimation problems with joint estimation of mechanistic and ML model parameters. It supports several ML ODE hybridization patterns, comes with a reference Python library, downstream tooling in Python/JAX (AMICI) and Julia (PEtab.jl), and a collection of real data benchmarks.
AI.result: Provides a standardized, reproducible framework for SciML parameter estimation with cross-ecosystem support and real-world benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: PEtab SciML facilitates reproducible and efficient scientific machine learning by offering a unified, interoperable specification and tooling across Python and Julia ecosystems.

title: Novel models of trait evolution via an expansion of Lande's fitness function: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process meets the Little Prince's boa
comment: Submitted to the Journal of the Society of Modeling and Theory in Population Biology
summary: Adaptive topographies form the foundation for much of our understanding of evolutionary change. Lande's 1976 influential paper on the adaptive topography of phenotypes demonstrated how the concept is inherent in both phenotypic and genetic models of evolution, and how the concept can be used to test evolutionary hypotheses given data. Here, we revisit and generalize Lande's original derivation of an equation analogous to Wright's genotypic adaptive topography to the case of two fitness components. A move to two fitness components yields novel predictions about the shape and mechanistic underpinnings of the adaptive topography. The optimum of this updated fitness function is a weighted average of the optima of the two fitness components, with weights given by the relative strengths of stabilizing selection on each component. Temporal or spatial heterogeneity in the strengths of selection for each fitness component create novel shapes (asymmetry, bi-modality, or lack thereof) of the overall fitness function, a possibility demonstrated with a case-study from the published literature. Finally, when combined with Lande's approach to generate an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model for the evolution of the average phenotype, our fitness formulation leads to a previously unrecognized family of stochastic differential equation models of trait evolution. These results provide mechanistic justification for non-Gaussian fitness functions (often observed in natural systems), provide a path for testing alternative models generating non-Gaussian fitness functions, and pave the way for future study of the interplay of ecological and evolutionary dynamics, such as in the study of evolutionary rescue.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes Lande's (1976) adaptive topography framework from a single fitness component to two fitness components, showing that the resulting fitness optimum is a weighted average of component optima, that heterogeneity in selection strength creates novel fitness function shapes (asymmetry, bi-modality), and that combining this with Lande's approach yields new stochastic differential equation (OU-type) models of trait evolution.
AI.motivation: Lande's adaptive topography framework is foundational in evolutionary biology, but the original derivation assumes a single fitness component. Real organisms often face multiple fitness components (e.g., survival and reproduction) with potentially different optima and selection strengths, so the framework needs generalization to capture more realistic evolutionary dynamics and to explain non-Gaussian fitness functions frequently observed in nature.
AI.method: The authors revisit and generalize Lande's mathematical derivation of the adaptive topography equation to the case of two fitness components. They derive a weighted-average optimum formulation where weights depend on relative stabilizing selection strengths. They also combine the generalized fitness function with Lande's approach to derive a new OU-type stochastic differential equation model, and illustrate the framework using a published case study.
AI.result: The generalized two-component fitness function produces novel adaptive topography shapes (asymmetry, bi-modality) under temporal or spatial heterogeneity in selection strengths. The framework leads to a previously unrecognized family of stochastic differential equation models of trait evolution, providing mechanistic justification for non-Gaussian fitness functions observed in natural systems.
AI.conclusion: The two-fitness-component generalization of Lande's adaptive topography offers novel predictions about fitness landscape shapes, provides a mechanistic basis for non-Gaussian fitness functions, enables testing of alternative models, and opens pathways for studying ecological-evolutionary dynamics such as evolutionary rescue.

title: Automatic bioinformatic software named entity recognition from literature
summary: Bioinformatics software and databases are essential components of modern life science research, yet their mentions in the scientific literature are often inconsistent and difficult to systematically identify at scale. The lack of a comprehensive and up-to-date catalog of bioinformatics resources hinders efforts toward automated biomedical knowledge extraction and streamlined data analysis. Here we present SNAIL, a hybrid named entity recognition framework designed to automatically identify bioinformatics software and database (SW/DB) names from biomedical texts. SNAIL integrates complementary lexical and semantic modeling strategies. The lexical component captures orthographic patterns and contextual cues characteristic of SW/DB names, while the semantic component leverages contextual embeddings generated by transformer-based language models such as SciBERT, combined with an explicit token-masking strategy to enhance entity-focused representations. A large training corpus was constructed automatically through a hybrid pipeline that integrates citation-hinted extraction with large language model-assisted distillation. Evaluation on two independent benchmark datasets and real-world research articles demonstrates that SNAIL substantially outperforms existing approaches, including domain-specific methods such as bioNerDS2 and general-purpose large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude. Applying SNAIL to large-scale literature analysis further reveals distinct journal-level preferences across bioinformatics subfields. These results demonstrate that SNAIL provides an accurate and scalable solution for identifying bioinformatics resources in scientific texts and enables systematic meta-analysis of tool usage and research trends.

AI.tldr: SNAIL is a hybrid named entity recognition framework that automatically identifies bioinformatics software and database (SW/DB) names from biomedical texts, combining lexical pattern matching with transformer-based semantic embeddings. It outperforms existing approaches on benchmark datasets and enables large-scale meta-analysis of tool usage in bioinformatics literature.
AI.motivation: Bioinformatics software and database mentions in scientific literature are inconsistent and hard to identify at scale due to the lack of a comprehensive, up-to-date catalog. This hampers automated biomedical knowledge extraction and streamlined data analysis.
AI.method: SNAIL integrates two complementary strategies: (1) a lexical component capturing orthographic patterns and contextual cues of SW/DB names, and (2) a semantic component using transformer-based contextual embeddings (e.g., SciBERT) with an explicit token-masking strategy. A large training corpus was built via a hybrid pipeline combining citation-hinted extraction with LLM-assisted distillation.
AI.result: SNAIL substantially outperforms existing approaches on two independent benchmark datasets and real-world research articles, including domain-specific methods (bioNerDS2) and general-purpose LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude). Large-scale application reveals distinct journal-level preferences across bioinformatics subfields.
AI.conclusion: SNAIL provides an accurate and scalable solution for identifying bioinformatics resources in scientific texts and enables systematic meta-analysis of tool usage and research trends.

title: Quantum Kernel Estimation for the Discovery of Early Lung Cancer Detection
summary:
Lung cancer screening with low-dose chest computed tomography reduces mortality, but its impact is limited by uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cell-free DNA (cfDNA) biomarkers offer a complementary approach, although early detection remains difficult because of lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals. We evaluated quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using DNA fragmentomics and DNA methylation. After feature selection, models were trained using 20- and 40-feature subsets. Features were encoded into quantum Hilbert space using angle and dense-angle feature maps with multiple entanglement strategies. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed with exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression and compared with an SVM model trained on the original features.
  This framework enabled systematic evaluation of how encoding and entanglement design affect classification. Across repeated held-out evaluations, quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature configurations improved AUC relative to a classical SVM baseline, suggesting effective capture of nonlinear cfDNA fragmentation structure. For methylation, the classical SVM achieved the highest AUC, although selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability. Overall, these results support quantum kernel methods as a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates quantum-classical hybrid machine learning for lung cancer detection using cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentomics and methylation data, comparing quantum kernel models (using various feature maps and entanglement strategies) against a classical SVM baseline, finding competitive performance with some quantum configurations improving AUC for fragmentomics.
AI.motivation: Lung cancer screening via low-dose CT is limited by uptake, adherence, and management challenges. Blood-based cfDNA biomarkers offer a complementary approach, but early detection is difficult due to lung cancer heterogeneity and high-dimensional, nonlinear molecular signals. The authors aim to explore whether quantum-classical hybrid machine learning can better capture these nonlinear patterns.
AI.method: Features were selected into 20- and 40-feature subsets. Quantum feature maps (angle and dense-angle) with multiple entanglement strategies encoded features into Hilbert space. Fidelity-based quantum kernels were computed via exact statevector simulation and integrated with precomputed-kernel SVM and kernel-PCA logistic regression, compared against a classical SVM baseline. The framework systematically evaluated how encoding and entanglement design affect classification with repeated held-out evaluations.
AI.result: Quantum-kernel models achieved competitive performance on both fragmentomics and methylation datasets. For fragmentomics, several 20-feature quantum configurations improved AUC relative to the classical SVM baseline. For methylation, the classical SVM achieved the highest overall AUC, though selected quantum models remained competitive and improved specificity in some cases. Increasing features from 20 to 40 did not consistently improve performance and often increased variability.
AI.conclusion: Quantum kernel methods represent a promising approach for cfDNA-based lung cancer detection, effectively capturing nonlinear fragmentation structure in some cases, though feature dimensionality and quantum circuit design choices require careful tuning.

title: Longitudinal Bayesian Learning of Continuous Disease Position across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progresses as a continuous biological process, whereas most existing neuroimaging-based artificial intelligence methods remain limited to discrete diagnosis or clinical score prediction from cross-sectional imaging. In this work, we propose Disease Continuum Positioning (DCP), a longitudinal Bayesian Learning framework that continuously estimates disease severity from longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Specifically, DCP models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable by jointly integrating longitudinal observations with weak clinical supervision, from which the proposed Disease Continuum Score (DCS) is derived to quantify an individual's position along the Alzheimer's disease continuum together with its associated uncertainty. Extensive experiments on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort demonstrate that DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. More importantly, comprehensive validation analyses show that DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion. These results suggest that DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores.

AI.tldr: DCP is a longitudinal Bayesian learning framework that continuously estimates Alzheimer's disease severity from DTI imaging by modeling disease progression as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable, yielding a Disease Continuum Score (DCS) with uncertainty estimates that outperforms existing methods and demonstrates strong clinical relevance.
AI.motivation: Existing neuroimaging-based AI methods for Alzheimer's disease are limited to discrete diagnosis or cross-sectional clinical score prediction, failing to capture the continuous biological progression of the disease.
AI.method: DCP is a longitudinal Bayesian learning framework that models disease severity as a low-dimensional probabilistic latent variable by jointly integrating longitudinal DTI observations with weak clinical supervision, from which a Disease Continuum Score (DCS) is derived with associated uncertainty.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the ADNI cohort show DCP consistently outperforms representative disease progression methods. Validation analyses demonstrate DCS accurately characterizes disease severity, exhibits strong clinical relevance, preserves longitudinal disease evolution, and predicts future disease conversion.
AI.conclusion: DCS provides a quantitative imaging-derived representation for continuous assessment of Alzheimer's disease progression beyond conventional diagnostic labels and clinical scores, offering a more nuanced view of the disease continuum.

title: Resource-Efficient Bio-Molecular Docking on a NISQ-era Digital Quantum Computer
summary: Molecular docking is a vital computational task in drug discovery, wherein the objective is to efficiently identify optimal binding poses between a ligand and a target receptor protein. Due to the combinatorial explosion of possible binding configurations, docking of large and flexible molecules remains a computationally intensive problem, especially at scale. Early studies have revealed that the molecular docking can be re-cast as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) problem on a compatibility graph to be solved classically. In this work, we proposed a hybrid quantum-classical approach for molecular docking leveraging the MVWCP formalism with a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy, which enables efficient encoding of classical binary variables with Bloch sphere vectors. We further prove that a global minimizer of the FBE objective can always be chosen to be a pure product state, thereby providing a rigorous justification for its optimization using a unitary variational circuit. The molecular docking problem is first mapped to a cost Hamiltonian that is minimized within a variational framework, optimized via a randomized imaginary time evolution (ITE)-inspired warm start, and gradient-based techniques. Finally, we also executed the circuit on an IBM quantum computer, underlying the feasibility and of quantum-assisted optimization for structure-based drug design and point towards the broader utility of advanced encoding techniques in quantum optimization for computational biology.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical approach for molecular docking that reformulates the problem as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP) and solves it using a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy. The method maps docking to a cost Hamiltonian optimized via randomized imaginary time evolution warm starts and gradient-based techniques, with demonstrations on an IBM quantum computer.
AI.motivation: Molecular docking is computationally intensive due to the combinatorial explosion of possible binding configurations for large and flexible molecules, especially at scale. While early work showed docking can be recast as an MVWCP on a compatibility graph, solving this classically remains challenging.
AI.method: The approach recasts molecular docking as a maximum vertex-weighted clique problem (MVWCP). They use a variational full-basis encoding (FBE) strategy that encodes classical binary variables with Bloch sphere vectors, prove that a global minimizer of the FBE objective can always be a pure product state, map the docking problem to a cost Hamiltonian minimized within a variational framework, and optimize it using randomized imaginary time evolution (ITE)-inspired warm starts with gradient-based techniques.
AI.result: The circuit was executed on an IBM quantum computer, demonstrating the feasibility of quantum-assisted optimization for structure-based drug design.
AI.conclusion: The work validates the practical feasibility of hybrid quantum-classical optimization for molecular docking and highlights the broader utility of advanced encoding techniques (FBE) in quantum optimization for computational biology applications.

title: Bringing analytic rigor to agentic AI for science: The Brain Researcher platform for neuroimaging data analysis
summary: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but an analytic output becomes a defensible claim only after alternatives are weighed and the claim is limited to what the evidence supports. Agents may reproduce failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success and optimization of imperfect criteria. We present Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness operating in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under rules for admissible analyses, required checks and claim scope. In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred. By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow, not after it.

AI.tldr: Brain Researcher is an agentic research harness that constrains AI agents' scientific analyses by enforcing rules for admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope. It improves tool-selection accuracy by 70.2 percentage points and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0% across seven models, while embedding methodological judgment within the workflow to prevent premature claims and selective analysis.
AI.motivation: AI agents can perform scientific analyses, but their outputs only become defensible claims after competing alternatives are weighed and claims are limited to what evidence supports. Without structure, agents reproduce human failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success, and optimization of imperfect criteria.
AI.method: Brain Researcher operates in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under explicit rules for admissible analyses, required checks, and claim scope. It employs multiverse analyses to expose analytic-choice sensitivity and integrates scientific review that classifies claims across categories including accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected, or deferred.
AI.result: In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and improved verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. Collaborator-led and self-evolving studies demonstrated multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the analytical workflow rather than applying it after the fact, enabling more defensible scientific claims from AI agents.

title: Flow Matching Meets 3D Curvilinear Structure Segmentation in Medical Imaging
comment: International Workshop on Machine Learning in Medical Imaging (MLMI 2026) @ MICCAI
summary: Segmentation of curvilinear anatomical structures in 3D medical images remains challenging due to complex topology, severe class imbalance, weak contrast, and large variations in structure morphology. While deep learning approaches for 3D curvilinear segmentation have been proposed, they are often tailored to specific anatomies or modalities, limiting generalization across clinical settings and leaving room for improvement. Recent generative models have shown the benefits of iterative prediction for structured segmentation tasks, yet diffusion-based methods suffer from computationally expensive sampling, hindering their use on high-resolution 3D volumes. We present 3D-CurvSegFlow, a flow matching-based model for 3D curvilinear structure segmentation. The model learns a continuous transformation from a simple source distribution to the target vascular representation, enabling progressive refinement of complex curvilinear geometries with efficient inference. We evaluate our method on Three public challenging datasets covering distinct anatomies and modalities: portal vein, cerebral vessel, and coronary arteries. Using a common architecture and training strategy across all tasks, our method outperforms general-purpose and vessel-specific approaches, with strong preservation of thin branches and vascular continuity. This work not only advances the state-of-the-art in 3D curvilinear segmentation but also opens new avenues for efficient, generalizable, and clinically applicable methods in medical image analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper presents 3D-CurvSegFlow, a flow matching-based model for 3D curvilinear structure segmentation in medical images. It learns a continuous transformation from a simple source distribution to target vascular representations, enabling progressive refinement of complex curvilinear geometries with efficient inference. Evaluated on three public datasets (portal vein, cerebral vessel, coronary arteries) across different anatomies and modalities, it outperforms general-purpose and vessel-specific approaches while preserving thin branches and vascular continuity, demonstrating strong generalization with a common architecture and training strategy.
AI.motivation: Segmentation of 3D curvilinear anatomical structures remains challenging due to complex topology, severe class imbalance, weak contrast, and morphological variations. Existing deep learning approaches are often task-specific to anatomies or modalities, limiting generalization. Diffusion-based generative methods offer iterative refinement benefits but suffer from computationally expensive sampling that hinders use on high-resolution 3D volumes.
AI.method: 3D-CurvSegFlow is a flow matching-based model that learns a continuous transformation from a simple source distribution to the target vascular representation, enabling progressive refinement of complex curvilinear geometries with more efficient inference than diffusion-based approaches. The model uses a common architecture and training strategy across all tasks.
AI.result: The method outperforms general-purpose and vessel-specific approaches on three public datasets covering distinct anatomies and modalities (portal vein, cerebral vessel, coronary arteries), with strong preservation of thin branches and vascular continuity.
AI.conclusion: The work advances the state-of-the-art in 3D curvilinear segmentation and opens new avenues for efficient, generalizable, and clinically applicable methods in medical image analysis.

title: Emergence of cooperation: A reputation-modulated reinforcement learning
summary: Reputation is widely recognized as a key mechanism for sustaining cooperation. However, most existing game-theoretic models treat reputation primarily as an external factor that modulates payoffs, interaction structures, or strategy update rules. In many social contexts, though, reputation operates primarily as information -- it shapes how individuals interpret their own experiences and assess the behavior of others. To bridge this gap, we propose a spatial prisoner's dilemma game grounded in the reinforcement learning paradigm, in which agents equipped with Q-learning integrate both individual and social information via a locally defined reputation metric to guide their decisions. Our results reveal that reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes the emergence of cooperative behavior, and we observe a discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection as the temptation increases. Cooperation spreads through the nucleation of cooperative clusters, whereas the disintegration of these clusters drives the system into an absorbing state of complete defection. Overall, this study demonstrates that reputation facilitates cooperation not only by providing direct incentives but also by reshaping the social information landscape that agents rely on for learning and adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a spatial prisoner's dilemma game where Q-learning agents use a locally defined reputation metric to integrate individual and social information. Results show reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes cooperation, with a discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection as temptation increases. Cooperation emerges via nucleation of cooperative clusters and collapses into complete defection when these clusters disintegrate.
AI.motivation: Existing game-theoretic models treat reputation as an external factor that modulates payoffs, interaction structures, or strategy update rules. However, in many social contexts reputation functions primarily as information that shapes how individuals interpret experiences and assess others' behavior. This gap motivates a new framework where reputation is integrated into the learning process itself.
AI.method: A spatial prisoner's dilemma game grounded in reinforcement learning, where agents equipped with Q-learning integrate individual and social information through a locally defined reputation metric to guide their decisions.
AI.result: Reputation-modulated learning significantly promotes cooperative behavior. A discontinuous phase transition from full cooperation to full defection is observed as temptation increases. Cooperation spreads via nucleation of cooperative clusters, while disintegration of these clusters drives the system into an absorbing state of complete defection.
AI.conclusion: Reputation facilitates cooperation not only by providing direct incentives but also by reshaping the social information landscape that agents rely on for learning and adaptation.

title: Climate change and human mobility will shape dengue emergence risk in Europe
summary: The risk of local arbovirus outbreaks in Europe is expected to increase due to climate change, as suggested by the multiplication of arbovirus outbreaks in the last decades. Europe has historically been a non-endemic region, making it vital to pinpoint which populations are potentially exposed -and under which conditions- so we can build truly robust epidemic preparedness capabilities. We introduce an integrated, multi-scale model that fuses a mechanistic transmission engine with a vector abundance framework, all embedded in a mobility-driven metapopulation system capturing human, vector, and air-traffic movement. To this end, we combine climate and population projections with mobility data to estimate and map dengue emergence risk in Europe throughout the 21st century. Additionally, we introduce a dedicated migration model that explores how climate-driven population redistribution could alter these risk estimates.Assuming the climate avoids major tipping points, model-derived risk indicators increase substantially under most emissions scenarios. While the spatio-temporal risk will remain largely driven by importation, our results indicate a gradual transition toward an environment-driven regime, particularly under the worst-case emissions scenario. To better anticipate and manage recurrent arbovirus outbreaks, our findings highlight the need to integrate mobility pathways and climate-driven population redistribution into predictive models of vector-borne disease emergence in temperate regions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an integrated multi-scale model combining mechanistic transmission dynamics, vector abundance frameworks, and mobility-driven metapopulation systems to estimate and map dengue emergence risk in Europe throughout the 21st century under climate change scenarios.
AI.motivation: Europe is historically non-endemic for arboviruses, but climate change is increasing outbreak risk. Robust preparedness requires identifying which populations are potentially exposed and under what conditions.
AI.method: The authors integrate a mechanistic transmission engine with a vector abundance framework within a mobility-driven metapopulation system capturing human, vector, and air-traffic movement. They combine climate and population projections with mobility data, and introduce a migration model to explore climate-driven population redistribution effects on risk.
AI.result: Model-derived risk indicators increase substantially under most emissions scenarios (excluding major climate tipping points). Risk remains largely importation-driven, but results indicate a gradual transition toward an environment-driven regime, especially under worst-case emissions scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Predictive models of vector-borne disease emergence in temperate regions must integrate mobility pathways and climate-driven population redistribution to better anticipate and manage recurrent arbovirus outbreaks.

title: Growth phases of an active tissue: determinate, indeterminate, and proportionate
summary: Growth may cease at a target size or continue throughout life: the determinate and indeterminate phenotypes. We develop an active viscoelastic continuum model of a tissue growing along one axis, in which cell division and death generate active stresses. We find two asymptotic states: one in which the tissue reaches a relative size fixed by its material parameters, and one in which it elongates linearly without bound. Which state is realised is set by the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus. The transition originates in a bound on the elastic stress the tissue can support: a sufficiently large activity can never be balanced. In a tissue made of parts with different material properties, the growing phase settles into fixed length proportions, set by the mechanical impedances of the parts rather than inherited; matching impedances to initial lengths preserves the proportions the tissue began with. Determinate, indeterminate and proportionate growth thus appear as regimes of one continuum mechanical framework.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an active viscoelastic continuum model for tissue growth along one axis, showing that determinate growth (reaching a fixed size) and indeterminate growth (unbounded elongation) emerge as distinct asymptotic regimes depending on the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus. The model also explains proportionate growth in heterogeneous tissues, unifying all three growth phenotypes in one framework.
AI.motivation: To understand how tissues choose between determinate growth (ceasing at a target size) and indeterminate growth (growing throughout life), and to explain how growth proportions are established in heterogeneous tissues. The authors aim to provide a unified mechanical framework that captures all growth phenotypes.
AI.method: The authors develop an active viscoelastic continuum model of tissue growing along one axis, where cell division and death generate active stresses. They analyze the asymptotic states of the model and examine the conditions under which each growth regime is realized, including the case of tissues composed of parts with different material properties.
AI.result: Two asymptotic states exist: one where tissue reaches a fixed relative size determined by material parameters (determinate growth), and one where it elongates linearly without bound (indeterminate growth). The transition is governed by the ratio of active stress to elastic modulus, arising from a bound on the elastic stress the tissue can support. In heterogeneous tissues, growing parts settle into fixed length proportions determined by mechanical impedances rather than inheritance, with matching impedances to initial lengths preserving initial proportions.
AI.conclusion: Determinate, indeterminate, and proportionate growth are unified as distinct regimes within a single continuum mechanical framework, where the relative activity level of the tissue dictates which growth phenotype emerges.

title: Decoding silent reading from non-invasive EEG
comment: 45 pages (including 12 pages of Supplementary Material), 11 figures (including 2 in Supplementary Material)
summary: Non-invasive decoding of inner speech faces a fundamental data problem: a corpus pairing brain activity with a person's spontaneous inner monologue cannot be collected, and the available proxy paradigms (cued repetitive and retrospectively reported generative inner speech) are slow to acquire, poorly time-locked, and subject compliance is unverifiable. We therefore treat silent reading as a scalable proxy task and ask how much lexical and semantic information a contrastive decoder can extract from it. We report an open-vocabulary analysis of approximately 240,000 word presentations recorded from a single densely-sampled participant across 393 runs (ca. 49 h) of 19-channel dry-electrode EEG. Words from continuous narrative text were presented in rapid serial visual presentation, with typography randomised on every trial to partially decorrelate word identity from low-level visual form. A convolutional EEG encoder, optionally followed by a causal transformer, was trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective to align short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model. Decoding, evaluated as word-grouped top-10 retrieval against permutation baselines, was reliably above chance, extended to mid-frequency and rare words, and scaled log-linearly with training-data volume with no sign of saturation. Removing occipital and posterior-temporal electrodes reduced the word-level gain by roughly one third but left context tracking unchanged. Control analyses separate word-level decoding from narrative context tracking and from a non-neural positional prior introduced by the transformer's positional embedding. These results establish that open-vocabulary word-level information is recoverable from EEG during silent reading, and that decoding is data-limited rather than saturated.

AI.tldr: Using ~240,000 word presentations from a single participant's 49-hour dry-electrode EEG recording during rapid serial visual presentation of continuous narrative text, this study trains a CLIP-style contrastive decoder with a convolutional EEG encoder and optional causal transformer to align EEG windows with LLM word embeddings, achieving above-chance open-vocabulary word decoding that scales log-linearly with data volume without saturation.
AI.motivation: Inner speech decoding faces a fundamental data problem: spontaneous inner monologue cannot be paired with brain recordings, and existing proxy paradigms (cued and retrospective generative inner speech) are slow, poorly time-locked, and have unverifiable compliance. Silent reading is proposed as a scalable, well-controlled proxy task to investigate how much lexical and semantic information can be recovered from EEG.
AI.method: A single participant read continuous narrative text in rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) with randomized typography to decorrelate word identity from low-level visual form. A convolutional EEG encoder (optionally followed by a causal transformer) was trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective to align short EEG windows with LLM hidden-state embeddings of the presented word. Decoding was evaluated via word-grouped top-10 retrieval against permutation baselines.
AI.result: Word decoding was reliably above chance, extended to mid-frequency and rare words, and scaled log-linearly with training data volume without saturation. Removing occipital and posterior-temporal electrodes reduced word-level gain by ~1/3 but left context tracking unchanged. Control analyses separated word-level decoding from narrative context tracking and a positional prior from transformer positional embeddings.
AI.conclusion: Open-vocabulary word-level information is recoverable from EEG during silent reading, and decoding performance is data-limited rather than saturated, suggesting further gains are possible with more data.

title: GENIE: Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics
summary: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic highlighted the ongoing risk infectious diseases pose to society and the value of reliable information on the likely future burden. When forecasting an epidemic at fine spatial resolution, traditionally used mechanistic compartmental model struggle to capture highly complex granular transmission dynamics, resulting in inaccurate and overconfident forecasts. However, detailed Agent-Based Models (ABMs), are challenging to calibrate and are too computationally expensive to use in real-time. Amortized simulation-based inference promises to overcome this difficulty by exploiting the power of machine learning (ML) to perform approximate forecasting at near-real-time using arbitrarily complex models of epidemics. In this work we introduce Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics (GENIE), a spatio-temporal ML-based framework for high-resolution forecasting of the burden of respiratory pathogens. GENIE is designed to reflect two key characteristics of outbreaks: (i) shared biological mechanisms across locations and (ii) location-specific characteristics affecting transmission dynamics. This results in the model architecture having two modules: (i) a Local Infection Encoder - which learns to represent disease dynamics shared across all locations and (ii) a Local Profile Encoder - which learns location-specific representations. Using simulations from a high-resolution spatio-temporal ABM, GENIE is trained to generate samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution of future epidemic trajectories. Benchmarked against established statistical and ML models, GENIE demonstrates superior performance across a range of measures including the timing and magnitude of peak hospitalisations.

AI.tldr: GENIE is a spatio-temporal ML framework using amortized simulation-based inference to forecast respiratory pathogen epidemics at high resolution, using a two-module architecture (shared disease dynamics encoder + location-specific encoder), trained on high-resolution ABM simulations and outperforming established benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional compartmental models struggle with fine-grained spatial epidemic forecasting due to oversimplified transmission dynamics, while detailed Agent-Based Models are too computationally expensive for real-time calibration and use. There is a need for a method that combines the fidelity of ABMs with the speed required for timely forecasting.
AI.method: GENIE is an ML-based framework employing amortized simulation-based inference, trained on high-resolution spatio-temporal ABM simulations. Its architecture consists of two modules: (i) a Local Infection Encoder capturing shared biological disease dynamics across locations, and (ii) a Local Profile Encoder learning location-specific transmission characteristics. Together they generate samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution of future epidemic trajectories.
AI.result: Benchmarked against established statistical and ML models, GENIE demonstrates superior forecasting performance across multiple measures, particularly in predicting the timing and magnitude of peak hospitalisations.
AI.conclusion: GENIE successfully bridges the gap between complex ABM fidelity and real-time forecasting feasibility, providing a scalable ML-driven approach for high-resolution epidemic forecasting of respiratory pathogens.
